When I read, I use my imagination. I can see the main character in my own way.

p2.t: I prefer films to books. I get bored when there are no pictures.
Then you should try comics! They have stories and pictures.

Very! It's cool and clean, and the trains have no drivers.

p1.t: Noura, you look tired. What happened last night?
Well, I was doing my homework when the doorbell rang.
Who was it?
My aunt and her five children! It was a big surprise. They arrived from Hail without calling.

p2.t: Oh no! Was your house ready for guests?
Not at all! The living room was in a mess, and my brothers were playing video games.
What did you do?
We got ready very quickly. Mum made coffee, and I tidied the room.
And did you finish your homework?
No, I didn't! We were talking until midnight.

It was a disaster! We were having lunch in the park when suddenly it started to rain.
Did you get wet?
Very wet! It was raining heavily, and our picnic things were in a mess.

p2.t: Was there thunder and lightning too?
Yes, lots! My little sister was crying, and Dad was looking for the car keys.
Oh no. What happened when you got home?
While we were changing our clothes, there was a power cut! We sat in the dark for an hour.
What a day! But I still love the rain.

Oh no! What were you doing?
I was riding down a hill when suddenly my wheel slipped on some wet sand.

p2.t: Did you hurt yourself badly?
Not really, but my knee was bleeding. A man ran over and asked, 'Are you OK?'
That was kind. Did he help you?
Yes. He had a first aid kit, so he cleaned my knee and put a plaster on it.
You were lucky.
I know! Next time I'll ride more slowly.

p2.t: Were you worried?
Very! We went back to the shoe shop, but it wasn't there.
So what did you do?
We asked a security guard. Luckily, a woman found my purse and took it to the information desk.

dialogue.scene: Lama asks her grandfather, Grandpa Saleh, to tell her a story from when he was a boy.

p1.t: Grandpa, tell me a story from when you were young.
All right. One day, when I was twelve, I was looking after our camels in the desert.
Alone?
Yes. At first, everything was fine. I was sitting under a tree when suddenly a sandstorm started.

p2.t: What did you do?
I couldn't see anything, and I got lost. I walked for hours.
Were you scared?
Very! Luckily, the camels knew the way home, so I followed them.
And in the end?
In the end, I got home at night. My mother was crying, but she was so happy to see me.

prompts.hint: Make a promise with 'I promise I'll …'.

prompts.q: It's a new white ball. What will you do after the match?
prompts.hint: Promise what you will do with the ball: 'I'll …'.

prompts.q: When will you give it back?
prompts.hint: Say a time, and make a promise with 'I won't …' too.

culture.title: Keeping Promises
points: An Arabic saying tells us that a promise is like a debt: you must keep it.
In Japan and the USA, children sometimes make a 'pinky promise' by holding their little fingers together.
In many cultures, people shake hands when they agree to do something.
qs: Why is it important to keep a promise?
Have you ever made a promise that was hard to keep?

3-2.exit: Make two promises to me: one with 'I'll' and one with 'I won't'.

3-3.objective: Today you will predict what your life might be like when you grow up.
3-3.warmup: What did you want to be when you were younger?

expressions.def: to become an adult
expressions.frame: When I grow up, I'll probably ___.

expressions.def: to start to be something
expressions.frame: I might become a ___ one day.

expressions.def: a person who designs machines, roads or buildings
expressions.frame: An engineer can build ___.

expressions.def: a place where people study after they finish school
expressions.frame: I'd like to study ___ at university.

expressions.def: something you really want to do one day
expressions.frame: My dream is to ___.

expressions.def: a person who plans and makes video games
expressions.frame: A game designer needs to be good at ___.

dialogue.scene: It's careers day at school. Reem and her friend Sara are talking about their future.

p1.t: Reem, what do you want to be when you grow up?
My dream is to become an engineer. I love building things.
Cool! Will you study at university here?
Probably. I'll study in Riyadh, and I might go abroad for a year too.

p2.t: What about you, Sara?
I'm not sure yet. I might become a game designer, or I might be a teacher.
A game designer? That's a great job! Will you make games for children?
Definitely! And I'll put a character called Reem in my first game.
Ha! I promise I'll play it every day.

dialogue.focus: I might become a game designer, or I might be a teacher.
qs: What does Reem want to become?
What will Sara put in her first game?

speakout.scene: I'm a reporter for a TV show called 'Kids of Today'. I'm asking children about their future.

prompts.q: What do you think you'll do when you grow up?
prompts.hint: Use 'I'll probably …' or 'I might …'.

prompts.q: Will you go to university? What will you study?
prompts.hint: Say how sure you are and name a subject.

prompts.q: Where do you think you'll live?
prompts.hint: Name a place and give a reason.

culture.title: New Jobs in Saudi Arabia
points: Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 plan aims to create many new jobs for young people.
There are now more jobs in tourism, technology, entertainment and sport.
Some jobs of the future don't exist yet, so children will need to learn new skills.
qs: Which job do you think will be popular in 2040?
Would you rather work in an office or outdoors? Why?

3-3.exit: Tell me two things you think you'll do when you grow up and one thing you might do.

3-4.objective: Today you will offer help to a friend and make promises to support them.
3-4.warmup: Who helps you when you have a problem?

expressions.def: words to tell someone not to feel bad or afraid
expressions.frame: Don't worry, I'll help you with ___.

expressions.def: to be sure that someone will help you
expressions.frame: You can count on me to ___.

expressions.def: to give something to someone for a short time
expressions.frame: I'll lend you my ___.

expressions.def: to not tell other people something private
expressions.frame: I promise I'll keep your secret about ___.

expressions.def: to help someone understand something
expressions.frame: I'll explain ___ to you after school.

expressions.def: a little afraid before something important
expressions.frame: I feel nervous before ___.

dialogue.scene: Lina was ill last week. Her friend Huda sees that she looks worried at school.

p1.t: Lina, are you OK? You look worried.
I missed three maths lessons last week. The test is on Sunday, and I'm really nervous.
Don't worry. I'll explain the lessons to you at break.
Really? Thank you so much!

p2.t: I'll lend you my notebook too. All the lessons are in it.
That's very kind. I promise I'll give it back on Sunday after the test.
No problem. You can count on me.
One more thing. Please don't tell the others I'm nervous.
Of course. I'll keep your secret. I won't tell anyone.

dialogue.focus: Don't worry. I'll explain the lessons to you at break.
qs: Why is Lina nervous?
What will Huda lend Lina?

speakout.scene: I'm your friend. I've got a big swimming race on Saturday, and I'm very nervous. Help me!

prompts.q: I'm so nervous! What can you do to help me?
prompts.hint: Offer help with 'Don't worry, I'll …'.

prompts.q: Will you come and watch the race?
prompts.hint: Make a promise with 'I promise I'll …'.

prompts.q: I fell in the pool at the last race. Please don't tell anyone!
prompts.hint: Promise to keep the secret with 'I won't …'.

culture.title: Friends Help Friends
points: The United Nations has an International Day of Friendship on 30 July.
An Arabic saying tells us that a true friend is there for you when you have a problem.
In many schools around the world, older students help younger ones as 'buddies'.
qs: How do you help your friends when they have a problem?
What makes someone a good friend?

3-4.exit: Your friend is nervous about a test. Make two offers or promises to help.

3-5.objective: Today you will make predictions about our planet and promise what you will do to help it.
3-5.warmup: What do you do at home to help the planet?

expressions.def: the air, water and land around us
expressions.frame: One way to help the environment is ___.

expressions.def: to use paper, plastic or glass again to make new things
expressions.frame: At home, we recycle ___.

expressions.def: to use more of something than you need
expressions.frame: I won't waste ___ any more.

expressions.def: to put a young tree in the ground
expressions.frame: I'd like to plant a tree in ___.

expressions.def: to stop a machine or a light working
expressions.frame: I promise I'll turn off the ___ when I leave the room.

expressions.def: I'm telling you that I will really do this
expressions.frame: For the planet, I promise I'll ___.

dialogue.scene: Nasser and his sister Shahad are making a poster for their school's Green Week.

p1.t: Our school wants every student to make a green promise. What's yours, Nasser?
I promise I'll turn off the lights and the air conditioner when I leave my room.
Good one. I won't waste water when I brush my teeth.
Do you think the world will be hotter in the future?
Scientists think it probably will. And there might be less water.

p2.t: Then let's do more. Our family could recycle plastic bottles.
Yes! And I'll ask Dad if we can plant a tree in the garden.
Trees are great for the environment. They'll give us shade too.
Let's write our promises on the poster and put it on the fridge.

dialogue.focus: I promise I'll turn off the lights and the air conditioner when I leave my room.
qs: What does Shahad promise to do?
What does Shahad want to ask Dad?

speakout.scene: I'm the head of our school's Green Club. We're making a 'Green Promise Wall', and I'd like your predictions and your promise.

prompts.q: What do you think our planet will be like in 2050?
prompts.hint: Make a prediction with 'will', 'won't' or 'might'.

prompts.q: What will you promise to do for the environment?
prompts.hint: Make two promises with 'I promise I'll …' and 'I won't …'.

prompts.q: What can our school do?
prompts.hint: Suggest one idea and say what will happen.

culture.title: The Saudi Green Initiative
points: The Saudi Green Initiative started in 2021.
It plans to plant ten billion trees across Saudi Arabia in the coming years.
Trees give shade, clean the air and help to keep cities cooler.
qs: Where would you like to plant a tree in your city?
Do you think people will use less plastic in the future? Why?

3-5.exit: Make one prediction about our planet and one green promise.

words.ex: Have you ever tried Japanese food?
I've never tasted camel milk.
Taste the soup before you add salt.
This chicken is very spicy!
Kabsa is a famous Saudi dish.
I've been to that restaurant once.

dialogue.t: Have you ever tried jareesh, Sam?
No, I've never eaten it. What does it taste like?
It's soft and warm. Here, taste some.
Mmm, it's good! It isn't spicy at all.
Have you ever eaten anything really spicy?
Yes, I tried a very spicy curry once. My mouth was on fire!

grammar.title: Have you ever …? / I've never …
grammar.ar: نستخدم Have you ever + التصريف الثالث للفعل لنسأل عن تجربة في أي وقت من الحياة، ونستخدم I've never + التصريف الثالث لنقول إننا لم نفعلها أبداً.
examples: Have you ever tried sushi? Yes, I have.
I've never eaten camel meat.
She has tasted jareesh once.

words.ex: I've been to Jeddah three times.
My uncle often travels abroad for work.
The journey from Riyadh to Jeddah is very long by car.
We took photos of the view from the mountain.
Our first night in the desert was unforgettable.
Dad has gone to Dammam. He'll be back on Sunday.

dialogue.t: Where have you been, Reem?
I've been to Taif with my family.
I've never been there. Was it a long journey?
Yes, but the view from the mountains was amazing.
Have you ever travelled abroad?
Yes, I went to Malaysia two years ago. It was unforgettable!
Where's your brother?
He's gone to Jeddah with my uncle.

grammar.title: been to / gone to
grammar.ar: has been to = ذهب وعاد. has gone to = ذهب وما زال هناك. وعندما نذكر وقتاً محدداً نستخدم الماضي البسيط: I went there last year.
examples: I've been to Taif. I went there last week.
My brother has gone to Jeddah. He isn't here.
Have you ever been to Dammam?

words.ex: I've already packed my bag.
Have you finished your homework yet?
Dad has just arrived home.
I packed my torch and a warm jacket.
It was dark, so I used my torch.
Mum wrote a shopping list.

dialogue.t: Have you packed your bag yet, Omar?
Yes, I've already packed it. Here's my list.
Where's your torch?
Oh no! I haven't found it yet.
Have you charged the camera?
Yes, I've just charged it. It's ready.

grammar.title: already / yet / just
grammar.ar: already وjust تأتيان بين have/has والفعل: I've already eaten. أما yet فتأتي في آخر السؤال أو الجملة المنفية: Have you eaten yet? I haven't eaten yet.
examples: I've already done my homework.
Have you packed your bag yet?
She's just called me.

words.ex: We fed the ducks at the park.
Don't touch the cat. It's asleep.
Wild animals live in forests, deserts and seas.
My little brother is scared of dogs.
We stood close to the giraffe.
We saw a shark at the aquarium.

dialogue.t: We went to a camel farm. Have you ever fed a camel?
No, I've never been close to a camel.
I touched a baby camel too!
Cool! I've seen sharks at the aquarium.
Weren't you scared of them?
No, there was thick glass between us!

grammar.title: Present perfect: I've seen … / Have you ever fed …?
grammar.ar: نكوّن المضارع التام بـ have/has + التصريف الثالث. بعض الأفعال شاذة: see → seen، feed → fed، be → been، eat → eaten.
examples: I've seen a desert fox.
Have you ever fed a camel?
My sister has never touched a snake.

words.ex: I've learned how to make tea.
He practises swimming three times a week.
His English has improved a lot.
My parents are proud of me.
I swam in the sea for the first time last summer.
Don't give up! You can do it.

dialogue.t: You swim really well now, Khalid!
Thanks! I've learned how to swim on my back.
When did you start lessons?
Last October. I nearly gave up, but I practised a lot.
Your swimming has really improved!
Yes, and last week I swam in the sea for the first time.

grammar.title: Present perfect or past simple?
grammar.ar: نستخدم المضارع التام عندما لا نذكر وقتاً محدداً: I've learned to swim. وعندما نذكر الوقت (last year, in 2023, when I was six) نستخدم الماضي البسيط: I learned last year.
examples: I've learned how to cook rice.
I learned it last summer.
When did you start? I started in October.

words.ex: I had an interview with our school's football coach.
Have you ever been on a plane?
That was the best trip I've ever had.
You went to the match? How was it?
Camping in the desert was a great experience.
I've flown on a plane twice.

dialogue.t: Dana, have you ever won a prize?
Yes, I have. I've won two prizes for drawing.
When did you win your first prize?
In Grade 4. It was the best day I've ever had at school.
Have you ever been on a plane?
Yes, twice. I flew to Egypt last year.
How was it?
It was an amazing experience!

grammar.title: Asking about experiences: present perfect + past simple
grammar.ar: نبدأ بسؤال المضارع التام Have you ever …؟ وإذا كانت الإجابة نعم نسأل عن التفاصيل بالماضي البسيط: When did you …? How was it?
examples: Have you ever won a prize? Yes, I have.
When did you win it? I won it last year.
It's the best trip I've ever had.

words.ex: I prefer football to basketball.
My brother is really into chess.
We play outdoors when the weather is nice.
In summer, we usually play indoors.
Reading a book before bed is relaxing.
The long walk was tiring.

dialogue.t: Do you want to go cycling this afternoon?
I prefer swimming to cycling. Cycling is too tiring.
But it's outdoors, by the sea.
The pool is indoors, so it's cool.
What are you into these days?
I'm really into drawing. It's relaxing.

grammar.title: prefer … to …
grammar.ar: نستخدم prefer + اسم أو فعل بـ ing، ثم to + اسم أو فعل بـ ing. لا نستخدم than مع prefer.
examples: I prefer juice to milk.
I prefer swimming to cycling.
She prefers reading to watching TV.

words.ex: I'd rather have a burger than pizza.
I'd prefer orange juice, please.
Lunch is the biggest meal in our house.
Let's share a big pizza.
Grilled chicken is a healthy choice.
Fried potatoes are tasty but not very healthy.

dialogue.t: Let's get a burger meal.
I'd rather have something healthy.
Would you rather have a shawarma or a salad?
I'd prefer the salad, I think.
Do you want to share some fries?
Yes, but only a small portion!

grammar.title: I'd rather + verb / I'd prefer + noun
grammar.ar: بعد I'd rather نضع الفعل في صيغته الأساسية: I'd rather have water. وبعد I'd prefer نضع اسماً أو to + فعل: I'd prefer water. / I'd prefer to sit outside.
examples: I'd rather have a salad.
I'd prefer juice, please.
Would you rather have rice or bread?

words.ex: I'd rather stay in a hotel than in a tent.
We spent three days at the seaside.
We saw colourful fish when we went snorkelling.
Let's go for a walk and get some fresh air.
The beach was too crowded.
Which do you prefer, the sea or the mountains?

dialogue.t: Which do you prefer, the seaside or the mountains?
I'd rather go to the seaside. I want to go snorkelling.
But the beaches are crowded.
Not all of them. Some are very quiet.
I'd prefer to go to the mountains for the fresh air.
Let's ask Dad. Maybe we can do both!

grammar.title: would rather … than … / I'd prefer to …
grammar.ar: I'd rather + فعل أساسي + than + فعل أساسي (أو اسم). أما I'd prefer فيأتي بعده to + فعل.
examples: I'd rather go to the seaside than to the mountains.
I'd rather swim than walk.
I'd prefer to stay in a hotel.

words.ex: I read a comic about a superhero.
'Treasure Island' is a famous adventure story.
Reading helps your imagination grow.
The main character is a boy called Sinbad.
The film had a happy ending.
I'd rather read the book than watch the film.

dialogue.t: Have you read this adventure story?
Yes! I'd rather read the book than watch the film.
Why?
When I read, I use my imagination.
I prefer films to books. I like pictures.
Then you should try comics!

grammar.title: Giving reasons for preferences
grammar.ar: بعد أن نقول ما نفضّله نذكر السبب بـ because، أو نقارن بين الشيئين: I prefer books to films because I can use my imagination.
examples: I prefer comics to long books because they have pictures.
I'd rather read the book than watch the film.
I find films more exciting than books.

words.ex: We took the metro to the city centre.
There's often a traffic jam in the morning.
The park is close, so we go on foot.
The new bus seats are very comfortable.
You can buy a metro ticket with a bank card.
I'd prefer to walk. It's a nice day.

dialogue.t: Shall we ask Dad to drive us to the museum?
I'd rather take the metro. There's always a traffic jam.
Is the metro comfortable?
Very! It's cool and clean.
Is the museum near the station?
Yes, it's ten minutes on foot.
OK, but I'd prefer to come back by car!

grammar.title: Comparing choices
grammar.ar: نقارن بين خيارين بالمقارنة (quicker, more comfortable)، ثم نقول ما نفضّله: The metro is quicker than the car, so I'd rather take the metro.
examples: The metro is quicker than the bus.
I'd rather walk than wait for the bus.
I prefer going by car to going by bus.

words.ex: There are three options for the trip.
I suggest the science centre.
I prefer farms to zoos.
I don't mind. Both options are fine.
We had a vote, and the farm won.
Most of us want to go to the farm.

dialogue.t: We have three options: a farm, a science centre or a water park.
I suggest the science centre.
I'd rather go to the water park. It's more fun!
But we went there last year.
What about the farm?
I don't mind the farm. Let's have a vote.
Fifteen for the farm! Most of us prefer the farm.

grammar.title: Choosing together
grammar.ar: نقترح بـ I suggest …، ونقول ما نفضّله بـ I'd rather / I prefer، وإذا كان الخياران مناسبين نقول I don't mind. ونصف رأي المجموعة بـ Most of us …
examples: I suggest the farm.
I'd rather go to the science centre.
I don't mind. Both options are good.

words.ex: We were eating dinner when the doorbell rang.
Grandma's visit was a big surprise.
The kitchen was in a mess after the party.
We got ready very quickly.
Our guests arrived at seven.
We gave our guests coffee and dates.

dialogue.t: You look tired. What happened last night?
I was doing my homework when the doorbell rang.
Who was it?
My aunt and her children! It was a big surprise.
Was your house ready for guests?
No! The living room was in a mess, and my brothers were playing video games.

grammar.title: Past continuous: was / were + -ing
grammar.ar: نستخدم الماضي المستمر لحدث كان مستمراً في وقت معيّن في الماضي: I was doing my homework at 8 pm. ونستخدم when + الماضي البسيط للحدث القصير الذي حدث في أثنائه.
examples: I was doing my homework when the doorbell rang.
My brothers were playing video games.
What were you doing at eight o'clock?

words.ex: It rained heavily all night.
There was thunder and lightning last night.
We didn't take umbrellas, so we got wet.
There was a power cut, and the lights went off.
Suddenly, the sky went dark.
While we were walking home, it started to rain.

dialogue.t: Did you enjoy the picnic, Sam?
No! We were having lunch when suddenly it started to rain.
Did you get wet?
Very wet! It was raining heavily.
Was there thunder and lightning?
Yes! And while we were changing our clothes, there was a power cut!

grammar.title: when and while
grammar.ar: نستخدم while مع الحدث الطويل (الماضي المستمر)، ونستخدم when مع الحدث القصير (الماضي البسيط): While we were walking, it started to rain. / We were walking when it started to rain.
examples: While we were having lunch, it started to rain.
We were walking home when we heard thunder.
Suddenly, the lights went off.

words.ex: My cousin fell off his scooter.
I slipped on the wet floor.
She hurt her arm playing basketball.
His knee was bleeding a little.
Mum put a plaster on my finger.
Are you OK? Let me help you.

dialogue.t: What happened to your knee, Saad?
I fell off my bike in the park.
What were you doing?
I was riding down a hill when my wheel slipped.
Did you hurt yourself badly?
Not really. A man cleaned my knee and put a plaster on it.

grammar.title: Past continuous + when + past simple
grammar.ar: الماضي المستمر يصف ما كان يحدث، والماضي البسيط بعد when يصف الحدث المفاجئ الذي قطعه: I was riding my bike when I fell off.
examples: I was riding my bike when I fell off.
She was running when she slipped.
What were you doing when it happened?

words.ex: He dropped his phone on the floor.
I was looking for my keys all morning.
I didn't notice the rain.
The security guard helped the lost boy.
Mum was worried because I was late.
Luckily, someone found my bag.

dialogue.t: Did you buy new clothes for Eid?
Yes, but while I was trying on shoes, I dropped my purse.
Oh no! Were you worried?
Very! We went back to the shop, but it wasn't there.
What did you do?
We asked a security guard. Luckily, a woman found it.

grammar.title: while + past continuous
grammar.ar: نستخدم while + الماضي المستمر لنصف ما كنا نفعله، ثم الماضي البسيط لما حدث فجأة: While I was shopping, I dropped my purse.
examples: While I was trying on shoes, I dropped my purse.
I was looking for my bag when I saw the guard.
Luckily, someone found it.

words.ex: I took my brother's bag by mistake.
We laughed at the funny film.
I was embarrassed when I fell in front of everyone.
My uncle tells great jokes.
The lights went off in the middle of the film.
Grandpa fell asleep in front of the TV.

dialogue.t: Why was everyone laughing about the play?
We were doing the play when Khalid fell asleep on the stage!
In the middle of the play?
Yes! Then he woke up and said the wrong line by mistake.
Was he embarrassed?
At first, but then he laughed too.

grammar.title: Telling a funny story
grammar.ar: نبدأ بالخلفية بالماضي المستمر (We were …ing)، ثم نذكر الحدث المضحك بالماضي البسيط، ثم نقول كيف كانت ردة فعل الناس.
examples: We were sitting in class when a bird flew in.
Everyone laughed.
I felt embarrassed, but then I laughed too.

words.ex: One day, a boy found a box in the sand.
At first, I was scared, but then I felt OK.
We stayed inside because of the sandstorm.
We got lost in the old part of the city.
Luckily, the shop was still open.
In the end, we found the way home.

dialogue.t: Grandpa, tell me a story!
One day, I was looking after our camels in the desert.
I was sitting under a tree when suddenly a sandstorm started.
What did you do?
I got lost. Luckily, the camels knew the way home.
And in the end?
In the end, I got home at night.

grammar.title: Story words
grammar.ar: نرتّب القصة بكلمات: One day (البداية) – At first – Suddenly (حدث مفاجئ) – Luckily (شيء جيد حدث) – In the end (النهاية). والخلفية بالماضي المستمر والأحداث بالماضي البسيط.
examples: One day, I was walking in the desert.
Suddenly, a sandstorm started.
In the end, I got home safely.

words.ex: Let's check the weather forecast before the trip.
It'll probably rain later.
Take a jacket. It might be cold.
Close the windows. A dust storm is coming.
The temperature will reach 40 degrees.
It's cloudy, but it isn't raining.

dialogue.t: What does the weather forecast say for Friday?
It will be sunny, but it might be windy in the afternoon.
Will there be a dust storm?
Probably not. It'll be cloudy in the afternoon.
What about the temperature?
About 28 degrees. Perfect for a picnic!

grammar.title: will / won't / might
grammar.ar: نستخدم will للتوقّع عندما نكون متأكدين تقريباً، وwon't (= will not) للنفي، وmight عندما لا نكون متأكدين: It might rain. وبعدها كلها الفعل في صيغته الأساسية.
examples: It will be sunny tomorrow.
It won't rain this week.
It might be windy in the afternoon.

words.ex: In the future, cars will drive themselves.
Robots will definitely help us at home.
A robot cleaned the floor.
I don't think we'll use paper money in the future.
Some cities are testing driverless cars.
Astronauts live and work in space.

dialogue.t: We need predictions about life in 2050.
I think everyone will have a robot at home.
Definitely! And people will probably travel in driverless cars.
Flying taxis might be normal in the future.
Will people go on holiday in space?
They might, but it'll be very expensive.

grammar.title: Predictions: how sure are you?
grammar.ar: متأكد 100%: will definitely. متأكد غالباً: will probably. غير متأكد: might. غالباً لا: probably won't / I don't think … will. لاحظ أن definitely وprobably تأتيان بعد will وقبل won't.
examples: People will definitely use robots.
We'll probably travel in driverless cars.
I don't think schools will disappear.

words.ex: I promise I'll call you tonight.
I won't be late again.
Dad always keeps his promises.
The bus arrived on time.
Please tidy up your toys.
You can trust me.

dialogue.t: Mum, can I go to Ziyad's house tomorrow?
What about your homework?
I promise I'll finish my homework first.
Last time, you didn't keep your promise.
I won't forget this time. You can trust me.
OK. But be home on time.

pages.text: Every morning before class, Noura and her best friend Huda watered the school garden. Their class was going to show their tomatoes at the school fair on Thursday. "These are the biggest tomatoes in the whole school," Huda said proudly.
But on Monday morning, three tomatoes were gone. On Tuesday, two more disappeared, and there were small holes in the soil. "Someone is stealing our tomatoes!" Noura cried.
The girls ran to tell their science teacher, Miss Amal. "Let's be detectives," she said with a smile. "Look carefully and write down everything you see."
Noura found tiny footprints near the garden wall. Huda found a piece of tomato under the old bench. "The thief is small," Noura said slowly, "and it's very hungry."

On Wednesday, the girls came to school very early and hid behind the classroom window. They waited and waited. Suddenly, something moved under the green leaves. It was round, brown and very, very slow.
It was a tortoise! He was eating a red tomato, and he looked very happy. Huda laughed so much that she almost fell over. "Our thief is the slowest thief in the world!"

At the fair, the girls didn't have the most tomatoes, but they had something better: a poster called "Our Garden Visitor" and a little wooden house for the tortoise. Everyone wanted to meet him, and the principal gave the class a prize for the most interesting project. The tortoise, now called Sultan, got his own corner of the garden, with one tomato plant just for him.

pages.text: Every winter, Omar's family went camping in the desert. This year, Grandpa Saleh came too. He was seventy-five and walked slowly, but his eyes were still sharp.
In the afternoon, Dad drove the car up a big sand hill. Suddenly, the wheels started to spin, and the car stopped. "We're stuck!" Dad said. Omar's little sister Lina looked worried.
Dad tried to call his brother, but there was no signal. "Don't worry," Grandpa said calmly. "When I was young, we didn't have phones. We had our hands and our heads."
Grandpa showed them how to let some air out of the tyres. Then everyone dug the sand away from the wheels. Mum and Lina put old carpets under the tyres, and Omar pushed with all his strength.
The car moved forward, and everyone cheered! But now the sun was going down, and Dad didn't know the way back to the camp. "Wait for the stars," Grandpa said with a smile.
When the sky was dark, Grandpa pointed to a bright star. "That's the North Star. Our camp is south of here, so we must drive away from it." Omar listened carefully and remembered every word.

An hour later, they saw the light of their tent. That night, around the fire, Omar asked, "Grandpa, can you teach me more about the stars?" Grandpa laughed and put his arm around him. "Of course. Every family needs someone who can find the way home."

stories.title: The Drone and the Lost Falcon

pages.text: Every Friday, Faisal visited his grandfather's farm outside Riyadh. Grandpa had a beautiful falcon called Barq, which means lightning. This time, Faisal brought something new: a small drone. It was his prize from the school science competition.
"Grandpa, look! My drone has a camera," Faisal said. Grandpa smiled. "Machines are fun, but they can't fly like Barq." Then he took the hood off the falcon's head and let it fly into the blue sky.

Suddenly, a strong wind started to blow. Barq flew higher and higher, and then he disappeared behind the hills. Grandpa called and called, but the falcon didn't come back. "It will be dark soon," he said quietly. "I'm worried."

Then Faisal had an idea. "My drone can fly faster than we can walk, and it can see everything from the sky!" He pressed a button, and the drone rose into the air with a loud buzz. Grandpa and Faisal watched the small screen together.

They saw sand, rocks and a long, empty road, but no falcon. The battery was getting low. "Only five more minutes," Faisal said nervously. Then Grandpa pointed at the screen. "Stop! What's that on the old palm tree?"

It was Barq! He was sitting near a small well, and he looked tired and thirsty. Faisal saved the place on the map, and they drove there in Grandpa's car. Grandpa held up his glove and whistled, and Barq flew down to him at once.

That evening, they sat outside with dates and Arabic coffee while Barq rested. "Your machine has good eyes," Grandpa laughed. "Next Friday, you can teach me how to fly it." Faisal smiled. "Only if you teach me how to train a falcon!"

stories.title: The Boy in the Dark Room

pages.text: Cairo, a thousand years ago. Yusuf was twelve, and he sold bread near the big mosque. Every morning, he saw a quiet man with ink on his fingers. People said the man was Ibn al-Haytham, a famous scientist.
One day, the man stopped at Yusuf's table. "I need a helper with fast feet and a good memory," he said. "Can you come to my house after lunch?" Yusuf felt nervous, but he said yes.

The scientist's room was completely dark. There was only one tiny hole in the wooden window. "Look at the wall," said Ibn al-Haytham. Yusuf turned and gasped, because there was a picture of the street on the wall, with people, camels and a palm tree!

"But everything is upside down!" Yusuf shouted. A man was walking on his head, and the camel's legs were in the sky. Ibn al-Haytham laughed. "Yes! Light travels in straight lines, so the picture turns over."

For many weeks, Yusuf helped him. He covered holes, carried lamps and wrote numbers in a notebook. Sometimes they made mistakes, but the scientist never got angry. "A mistake is a teacher too," he said.

One evening, Yusuf asked, "Why do you work so hard?" Ibn al-Haytham closed his book. "Many people believe things without checking them. I want to test every idea with my own eyes." Later, he wrote about all their experiments in a big book about light.

Many years later, Yusuf became a teacher himself. He showed his students a dark room with one tiny hole. "This idea is the grandfather of every camera," he told them with a smile. "And it started with a curious man and a boy who sold bread."

stories.title: The River That Came at Night

pages.text: Every winter, Faisal's family drove into the desert for a weekend camp. This year, his cousin Sami came too, and he wanted to choose the camping place. "Here!" he shouted, pointing at a wide, flat valley. "The sand is soft, and there are no rocks!"
Grandfather looked up at the sky. Above them it was clear and blue, but far away, over the mountains, there were dark grey clouds. "We shouldn't stay in this valley tonight," he said quietly.

Sami laughed. "But it isn't raining here, Grandfather! It's sunny." Faisal remembered a lesson from school. "When it rains in the mountains, the water can travel a long way," he explained. "It runs into dry valleys like this one, and it moves very fast."

Sami wasn't happy, but he helped carry the tents up a small hill nearby. They made a fire, drank sweet tea and watched the stars. Far away, lightning flashed silently in the distance, like a giant camera.
In the middle of the night, a strange noise woke Faisal. It sounded like a huge train coming closer and closer. He grabbed his torch and ran outside with Sami and Grandfather.

Below them, a brown river was rushing through the valley, carrying sand, stones and branches. The flat place where Sami wanted to camp was completely under water. Sami's face went white. "We were going to sleep there," he whispered.

In the morning, the water was gone, and the air smelled fresh and clean. A rainbow appeared over the wet sand. "Next time," Sami said with a smile, "I'll look at the sky first — and I'll listen to Faisal and Grandfather!"

pages.text: Every winter, Reem visited her grandfather's old mud house in the village of Ushaiger. The best thing in the house was the wooden front door. It was covered with red, yellow and green triangles, but the colours were faded and old. "My father painted this door seventy years ago," Grandpa said proudly.

One day, Reem's art teacher announced a competition. "Make something that shows your family's history," Miss Hana said. Reem knew immediately what she wanted to do. "Grandpa, can I paint the old door again?" she asked. "Yes," he smiled, "but you must use the same colours."

First, Reem cleaned the door very carefully with a soft brush and warm water. It was slow work, and her arms hurt. Then, under the dust in the bottom corner, she noticed something strange. There were tiny Arabic letters, painted in dark blue.

Reem read the letters slowly: "Noura." Grandpa put on his glasses and looked closely. His eyes became wet. "Noura was my mother," he whispered. "Everyone always said my father painted this door, but it was her!"

For two weeks, Reem mixed her colours and painted every triangle, just like her great-grandmother. On the last evening, while she was finishing the final line, dark clouds suddenly filled the sky. "It's going to rain!" Grandpa shouted. Together they carried the heavy door inside just before the storm began.

On competition day, the bright door stood in the school hall. The judges were curious about the small blue name in the corner. Reem told them the story of Noura, the woman nobody remembered. The whole hall went quiet as they listened.

Reem won first prize, but that was not the best moment. Back at home, Grandpa picked up a thin brush and dipped it in dark blue paint. Next to "Noura", he carefully wrote a new name: "Reem." "Now the door has two artists," he said, and they both laughed.

stories.title: The Boy with the Blue Cap

pages.text: Faisal loved Saturday mornings in his grandfather's clock shop in old Jeddah. Hundreds of clocks ticked on the walls, but one tall wooden clock in the corner was always silent. "It stopped many years ago," Grandpa Salem said. "Please don't touch the key."

One morning, Grandpa went to the mosque next door to pray, and Faisal was alone. He looked at the small golden key in the old clock. He only wanted to see it work, so he turned the key three times. Suddenly the room filled with bright light, and the floor began to shake.

When the light disappeared, the shop looked different. There were no phones, no computers and only a few clocks. Outside, men in white thobes were carrying boxes from the port, and an old radio was playing. A calendar on the wall said 1975!

In the corner, a thin boy was sitting next to the same tall clock, and he was crying. "I broke my father's clock, and he's coming back soon," he said. "My name is Salem." Faisal's mouth fell open, because this boy was his grandfather!

Faisal took off his blue cap and sat down next to him. "My grandpa... I mean, someone taught me how to fix clocks," he said. Together they opened the back of the clock and found a small spring in the wrong place. Faisal moved it carefully, and tick, tock, the clock started working again!

Salem's eyes shone. "When I grow up, I'm going to fix clocks for everyone," he said. Just then, the bright light came back, and Faisal quickly held the golden key. A second later, he was standing in the modern shop again, but his blue cap was gone.

Grandpa came in and smiled at the ticking clock. "So, you met him," he said quietly, and he opened an old drawer. Inside was a faded blue cap. "A kind boy left this here fifty years ago," Grandpa said, "and I've waited a long time to give it back."

pages.text: Every Friday morning, Faisal and his family went to the beach near Jeddah. His little sister Noura liked building sandcastles, but Faisal liked looking for crabs between the rocks. That morning, the sea was calm and blue, and the sun was already hot.
Suddenly, Faisal saw something moving near the water. "Noura, look! What's that?" he shouted. It was a young sea turtle, and an old fishing net was wrapped tightly around its front leg.

The turtle looked tired, and it couldn't swim. "Don't touch it with your hands," said Dad. "I'm going to call the marine centre, because they know what to do." While they waited, Faisal stayed next to the turtle and kept it wet with seawater from his bucket.

Twenty minutes later, two workers from the centre arrived with a big box and special scissors. Carefully, they cut the net away from the turtle's leg. "You found her just in time," one of them told Faisal. "She's very lucky."

Faisal looked along the beach, and now he saw other things too: plastic bottles, bags and pieces of old net. "Where does all this rubbish come from?" asked Noura. "From people," the worker answered sadly. "Turtles sometimes think plastic bags are jellyfish, so they eat them."

On Sunday, Faisal told his class about the turtle, and his teacher, Mr Saleh, had an idea. "Let's clean the beach together next weekend," he said. Thirty students and their families came with gloves and big bags. Together, they collected more than two hundred kilos of rubbish!

A month later, the marine centre invited Faisal's family back to the beach, and the workers put the turtle gently on the sand. Her leg was strong again, and she walked slowly into the waves. "Goodbye, little friend," Faisal said with a smile. "We'll keep your home clean."

questions.q: What was wrapped around the turtle's leg?
options: A piece of rope from a boat

questions.q: Why did Faisal put seawater on the turtle?
options: To keep it wet and safe
To wash the sand off his bucket

options: Because they think the bags are jellyfish

pages.text: Every day after school, Lama stopped at Uncle Saleh's small shop to buy a juice. He always smiled and gave her a date for free. But one afternoon, he wasn't smiling. He was holding a letter and looking at it sadly.
"What's wrong, Uncle Saleh?" Lama asked. "My eyes are getting worse," he said quietly. "My grandson Khalid studies in Canada, and he sends me letters. But I can't read them anymore."
Lama thought for a moment. "I can read them for you," she said. "I'll come every day after school." The old man's face became bright. "Really? You're very kind, my daughter."

The next day, Lama opened a box full of letters. Some were very old, and some were new. She read them slowly and clearly. Uncle Saleh laughed at Khalid's funny stories about snow and long, cold winters.

Then Lama opened the last letter and stopped. "Uncle Saleh, listen! Khalid is coming home. His plane lands tomorrow at five o'clock!" The old man stood up quickly. "Tomorrow? But who will take me to the airport?"
That evening, Lama told her father everything. "Of course we will help," he said. "Kindness is a gift that grows." The next afternoon, they drove Uncle Saleh to the airport.

When Khalid saw his grandfather, he ran and hugged him tightly. "Grandfather, I wrote to you so many times. Why didn't you answer?" Uncle Saleh pointed at Lama and smiled. "Now I have a reader, and from tomorrow, she will help me write back to you."

questions.q: Why couldn't Uncle Saleh read Khalid's letters?
options: He was too busy in his shop.
The letters were in a different language.

questions.q: Where does Khalid study?
"He hugged him tightly." What does "tightly" mean here?
How did Lama's father help?
options: He bought juice for Uncle Saleh.
He drove Uncle Saleh to the airport.

questions.q: Why didn't Uncle Saleh answer Khalid's letters before?
options: He couldn't read them, so he didn't know what they said.

pages.text: Every winter, Omar's family went camping in the desert near AlUla. This year, Grandpa brought his young camel, Najma. "She's fast, but she's very curious," Grandpa said with a smile. That night, he showed Omar how to find the North Star.

On the second afternoon, the sky turned orange and a strong wind started to blow. Everyone ran into the tents while sand flew everywhere. When the storm stopped, Najma's rope was on the ground, and Najma was gone.

"We have to find her before dark," said Grandpa. Omar and his sister Lama followed him with water bottles and a torch. The wind had covered most of the footprints, but Lama noticed a few small ones near the rocks.

The tracks led them into a narrow valley between tall red rocks. On the walls, Omar saw old drawings of camels and people. "These are thousands of years old," Grandpa whispered. Then they heard a soft, sad sound.

Najma was standing behind a big rock, and her leg was caught in an old, broken fence. Grandpa spoke to her quietly while Omar carefully pulled the wire away. Najma was free, and she pushed her nose into Omar's shoulder.

By now the sun had gone down, and Grandpa's phone had no signal. "Which way is the camp?" Lama asked nervously. Omar looked up and remembered Grandpa's lesson: find the bright star in the north, then keep it on your right.

They walked slowly under the stars until they saw the warm light of the campfire. Mum hugged everyone, and Dad gave them hot tea and dates. "You didn't need my phone tonight," Grandpa told Omar. "You had the sky."

questions.q: What happened to Najma during the storm?
options: She ran away from the camp.

questions.q: Who noticed the small footprints near the rocks?
In the story, what does "narrow" mean?
Why couldn't Grandpa use his phone to find the way back?
options: He left it in the tent.

questions.q: What does Grandpa mean when he says, "You had the sky"?
options: Omar liked looking at the stars for fun.
Omar used the stars to find the way back.

pages.text: Every summer, Yousef visited his grandfather on the Farasan Islands. One evening, they were walking on the beach with his sister, Noura, when Grandpa stopped suddenly. "Look at the sand," he whispered. "Something is moving."
Tiny animals were climbing out of a hole in the sand. "They're baby sea turtles!" Noura said excitedly. "Yes, and they must get to the sea quickly, before the birds find them," Grandpa explained.
But the babies were not going toward the water. They were walking toward the bright lights of a new café behind the beach. "Why are they going the wrong way?" asked Yousef.

"Baby turtles follow the light of the moon on the sea," said Grandpa. "But tonight the café lights are brighter than the moon, so the babies are confused." Noura looked at the café, and suddenly she had an idea.

She ran to the café and spoke politely to the owner, Mr. Khalid. "Excuse me, could you turn off your lights for a few minutes? Some baby turtles are in danger." Mr. Khalid looked surprised, but he went outside to see.

When he saw the tiny turtles, he quickly switched off every light. Now the moon was shining on the water, and the babies turned around. Yousef and Grandpa walked carefully beside them and chased away a hungry seagull.

One by one, forty-two little turtles reached the waves and swam away. The next week, Mr. Khalid put up a new sign: "Turtle Beach – Please Keep It Dark." "Maybe one day these turtles will come back here to lay their own eggs," said Grandpa with a smile.

questions.q: Where was Yousef spending his summer?
Why were the baby turtles going the wrong way?
options: The café lights were brighter than the moon

questions.q: In the story, "confused" means:
What did Noura do to help the turtles?
options: She carried them to the sea
She asked the café owner to turn off the lights

questions.q: Why did Mr. Khalid put up a new sign?
options: He wanted to sell more drinks
He wanted to protect the turtles in the future
He wanted to close the café

pages.text: Every winter, Sara and her grandfather drove into the desert near AlUla. "The city lights hide the stars," Grandpa said. "Out here, the sky is ours." They put a small telescope on the cold sand.

This year was different. Sara's uncle Khalid was an astronaut, and he was living on the International Space Station for six months. "Can we see him from here?" Sara asked. Grandpa smiled and checked the time on his phone. "Wait and watch the west."

At 7:42, a bright light appeared above the rocks. It didn't flash like a plane, and it moved faster than any star. "That's the space station!" Grandpa said. "It travels around the Earth sixteen times every day."

Sara jumped up and turned on her torch. She waved it left and right, again and again, and shouted, "Uncle Khalid! We're down here!" Then, after only five minutes, the light disappeared behind the mountains.
"He couldn't see my torch, could he?" Sara said quietly. "The Earth is too big." Grandpa put his arm around her. "Maybe not," he said, "but he knows we're looking."
Two days later, Sara's mother called her to the computer. There was a message from space! Uncle Khalid had sent a photo of the dark desert with a tiny dot of light in the middle.

"I took this when we flew over AlUla," he wrote. "I'm sure that little light was someone waving at me." Sara printed the photo and put it above her bed. Now, when she looks up at the night sky, she knows the sky is looking back.

questions.q: Where did Sara and her grandfather go every winter?
How did they know the bright light was not a plane?
options: It didn't flash and it moved very fast

questions.q: "The light disappeared behind the mountains." What does "disappeared" mean?
Why was Sara sad after the space station went away?
options: She thought her uncle couldn't see her torch

questions.q: Why do you think Sara put the photo above her bed?
options: Because her mother told her to
Because it made her feel close to her uncle

pages.text: Every afternoon, Omar and his friends played football on the empty ground behind their street. Almost every afternoon, the ball flew over the high wall into Mr. Hamad's garden. Mr. Hamad never smiled, so the boys were afraid to knock on his door.

One day, the school team got bad news. Their coach was moving to another city, just two weeks before the big match against Al-Noor School. "Who will train us now?" Omar asked sadly. That evening, the ball went over the wall again.
This time, Omar knocked on the door himself. Mr. Hamad opened it, holding the ball. Behind him, Omar saw an old photo of a young player lifting a gold cup. "Is that you?" Omar asked in surprise.
"Yes, a long time ago," said Mr. Hamad quietly. "I played for the national team until I hurt my knee." Omar took a deep breath. "Could you help our team, please? We don't have a coach anymore."

Mr. Hamad was very strict. The boys ran, passed and practised every day after school, even when it was hot. "Stop kicking the ball so high!" he told them. "Keep it low and pass to each other, because a team is stronger than one player."

On the day of the match, Al-Noor scored first, and Omar's team looked worried. Then they remembered Mr. Hamad's words. Omar passed low to Khalid, Khalid passed to Yusuf, and Yusuf scored! In the last minute, Omar scored the winning goal.
After the match, the boys ran to Mr. Hamad, and for the first time, he smiled. "You can kick the ball into my garden any time now," he laughed. "But come and get it yourselves, and stay for tea!"

questions.q: Where did the ball often go?
Why did the team need a new coach?
options: Their coach was moving to another city

questions.q: What did Omar see behind Mr. Hamad?
options: A photo of a young player with a cup

questions.q: In the story, "strict" means:
options: asking people to follow rules and work hard

questions.q: Why did Omar's team win the match?
options: They kicked the ball very high
They passed the ball and played as a team
The other team did not come

stories.title: The Parrot Who Kept a Secret

pages.text: Every afternoon at four o'clock, Grandpa's parrot, Zaytoon, disappeared from his cage. But at six o'clock, the little green bird was always back inside, and the door was shut again. "This is a real mystery," Lama told her brother Saad.
"Maybe Grandpa forgets to close the door," said Saad. But Grandpa shook his head and laughed. "I always sleep after Asr prayer, children. I don't touch that cage!"

The next day, Lama hid behind the curtain with her notebook. At exactly four o'clock, Zaytoon pushed the small metal hook up with his beak. The door opened, and he flew out of the open kitchen window!

Lama and Saad ran up to the roof as fast as they could. They saw a flash of green land on the balcony next door. "That's Umm Khalid's house," Saad whispered. "She moved there last month, and we've never met her."
At six o'clock, Zaytoon came home with a tiny piece of date on his feathers. Then he said a new word: "Delicious! Delicious!" Lama smiled and wrote another clue in her notebook.

That evening, the children visited Umm Khalid with their mother. The old lady laughed when she heard the story. "So he's your bird! I live alone, and every afternoon he visits me. He talks to me while I drink my tea, and I give him dates."

Now Zaytoon doesn't need to escape anymore, because Umm Khalid comes to Grandpa's house for tea every afternoon. Grandpa and his new friend tell stories, and the parrot shouts, "Delicious!" Lama closed her notebook and wrote two words on the last page: Case closed.

How did Zaytoon open the cage door?

Something that helps you find the answer to a mystery

options: He ate food in the kitchen

options: She wanted to buy a parrot
She lived alone and enjoyed his company
She wanted to teach him to fly

pages.text: Yousef was doing his homework on the roof when he heard a soft noise. A grey pigeon was sitting behind the water tank. It looked very tired, and there was a small blue ring on its leg.
Yousef gave the bird some water, but he didn't know what to do next. "Maybe Hamad knows about birds," he thought. Hamad was the new boy in his class. He was quiet and always sat alone at break time.

The next morning, Yousef walked over to Hamad's desk. "I found a pigeon with a ring on its leg," he said. Hamad's eyes became bright. "That's a racing pigeon! My grandfather keeps them in Taif. Can I see it?"

After school, Hamad came to Yousef's house with his father. He held the bird gently and looked at the ring carefully. "There are numbers here," he said. "Pigeon clubs write them, so people can find the owner."

Hamad called his grandfather and read the numbers to him. Then he laughed loudly, and it was the first time Yousef heard him laugh. "Grandpa says this is his pigeon! Her name is Sahaba, and she got lost in a storm last week."

On Friday, Hamad's grandfather drove from Taif to collect Sahaba. He thanked Yousef and invited both boys to visit his farm in the holiday. "A pigeon always finds its way home," he said with a smile. "And sometimes it brings friends together too."

Now Yousef and Hamad sit together at break time every day. They are planning their trip to Taif and reading books about birds. And when a grey pigeon flies over the school, they always look up and wave.

options: On the roof of his house

options: In a soft and careful way

options: Because the teacher told him to
Because he thought Hamad might know about birds

options: Happy, because he had a new friend
Angry, because he lost the pigeon
Bored, because he had nothing to do

pages.text: Faisal loved science, but his school project was a big problem. "Make something useful from nature," his teacher said. He had no ideas, and the science fair was next week.

On Friday, Faisal's family drove to the desert for a picnic with Grandpa. In the afternoon, the sun was very hot, and his little sister Reem dropped her water bottle in the sand. "Don't worry, we have more," said Grandpa. "But long ago, people in the desert had to find water in clever ways."
Grandpa dug a small hole in the sand and put a cup in the middle. Then he covered the hole with a plastic sheet and put a small stone on top. "Wait and see," he said with a smile.

Faisal was curious. "How can dry sand give us water?" he asked. "The sun warms the sand, and tiny bits of water go up into the air," Grandpa explained. "When they touch the cool plastic, they turn into drops again."
After two hours, Faisal lifted the edge of the plastic carefully. Small drops of water were running down to the stone and falling into the cup! "It's like a little rain machine!" Reem said happily.
Faisal took photos and wrote notes in his notebook. At home, he built a model of the water catcher and made a colourful poster. He called his project "Grandpa's Desert Rain."

At the science fair, many students and teachers stopped at his table to ask questions. Faisal won second prize, but he was happy about something more important. He gave the shiny medal to Grandpa and said, "This is yours too."

questions.q: What did Reem drop in the sand?
What did Grandpa put on top of the plastic sheet?
In the story, "curious" means...
Where did the water drops form?
Why did Faisal give his medal to Grandpa?
options: Because he didn't like second prize
Because Grandpa gave him the idea for the project

pages.text: Noura and her little brother Salem went camping in the desert with Grandpa. The red sand was soft and warm under their feet. Grandpa put up the tent, and the children collected dry wood for the fire.

That evening, a strange low sound came from the biggest dune. "Is it a monster?" Salem whispered. Grandpa laughed and poured the tea. "No, the sand is singing. When the wind moves the sand on that dune, it makes music."
The next morning, their small goat, Bunduq, was missing. Noura found tiny tracks going up the dune. "We'll find him and come back soon," she told Salem, and they started to climb.
At the top, Bunduq was eating a little green plant. But suddenly the wind became stronger, and the sky turned orange. "A sandstorm!" Noura shouted. Now they couldn't see the tent or the car.

Noura covered her face with her scarf and tried to stay calm. Then she heard it: the deep song of the dune, on her left. "Grandpa's tent is next to the singing dune," she said. "If we follow the music, we can get back."

They walked slowly, holding hands and Bunduq's rope, with the song always on their left. The sand hit their arms, but they didn't stop. After a few minutes, they heard another sound. It was Grandpa's car horn!

Grandpa ran to them and held them tightly. "You were clever and brave," he said, "but next time, tell me before you go anywhere." Later, under the bright stars, Noura smiled. "The desert helped us, Grandpa. It sang us home."

questions.q: What did the children collect at the camp?
Why did the dune make a sound?
What does "missing" mean in the story?
options: Not in its place and lost

questions.q: How did Noura know which way to walk in the sandstorm?
options: She listened to the singing dune

questions.q: What did Grandpa want the children to learn?
options: To tell an adult before going away
To never camp in the desert

stories.title: The Parrot Who Rang the Bell

pages.text: Faisal's family had a green parrot called Zaytoon. Zaytoon was very clever, but he only said one word: "Hello!" Faisal wanted to teach him more words before the big family dinner on Friday.

Every day after school, Faisal sat next to the cage and practised with him. "Say 'Welcome'," he said slowly. Zaytoon moved his head from side to side and said nothing. "You're a lazy bird!" Faisal laughed.
On Wednesday, the doorbell started ringing again and again. Dad ran to the door, but nobody was there. Ten minutes later, it rang again, and Grandma hurried to open it. Again, the street was empty.

"Maybe the neighbours' children are playing a joke on us," Dad said. He looked worried. Then Faisal saw something strange. Zaytoon opened his beak, and out came a perfect "Ding-dong!" Faisal laughed so hard that he fell onto the sofa.

On Friday, the house was full of uncles, aunts and cousins. Every few minutes, Zaytoon made the doorbell sound, and someone jumped up to open the door. Uncle Saad opened it five times. "This door is busier than the airport!" he said.

Dad ordered kabsa from his favourite restaurant, but the food was very late. Everyone was hungry. "Where is the delivery man?" Grandma asked. Suddenly there was another "Ding-dong!" and nobody moved. "It's only the parrot," Uncle Saad said.

But this time, a loud voice came from outside: "Hello? Your food is getting cold!" Everyone ran to the door at once. From his cage, Zaytoon shouted, "Welcome! Welcome!" and the whole family laughed until they cried.

questions.q: What word could Zaytoon say at the start of the story?
Who was really making the doorbell sound on Wednesday?
In the story, "hurried" means:

pages.text: Every Friday, Yousef went sailing with his grandfather, Jaddi Hamad, from Farasan Island. Grandfather knew every coral reef in the Red Sea. "The sea is a good friend," he always said, "but you must listen to it."
One afternoon, they went farther than usual to look for dolphins. Suddenly, the engine coughed and stopped. Grandfather tried again and again, but nothing happened. The sun was going down.
"Can we call Dad?" Yousef asked. He looked at his phone, but there was no signal. "Don't worry," Grandfather said calmly. "We have water, dates and a torch. And we have the sky."

Soon it was dark. When Yousef put his hand in the water, the sea began to shine with thousands of tiny blue lights. "They are very small sea animals," Grandfather explained. "When something moves near them, they glow."

Then Grandfather pointed up. "That bright star never moves. It is the North Star. Our island is south of us, so we must go the opposite way." The wind was blowing gently, so they put up the small sail.

For two hours, they sailed slowly through the dark water. Then Yousef saw a light far away, and it was flashing. "The lighthouse!" he shouted. Grandfather smiled. "You were the captain tonight, Yousef."

Near the harbour, Dad was waiting in another boat with a big lamp, and he hugged them both. That night, Yousef couldn't sleep, so he drew the North Star in his notebook. Next to it, he wrote: "Listen to the sea, and look at the sky."

questions.q: Why did Yousef and his grandfather go farther than usual?
Why couldn't Yousef call his dad?
options: He forgot his phone at home

questions.q: What made the sea shine with blue lights?
In the story, what does "opposite" mean?
Why did Grandfather say, "You were the captain tonight"?
options: Because Yousef saw the lighthouse and helped them get home

pages.text: Lina's grandfather, Jaddi Saleh, lived with her family in Jeddah. He was kind and funny, but he could not hear very well anymore. When his friends knocked on the door, he often didn't hear them, and they went home sad.
One morning, Ms. Noura made an announcement. "Next week we will have an invention fair," she said. "Make something that helps a person you love." Lina smiled, because she knew her idea at once.

Every evening, Lina worked at the kitchen table with an old bell, a battery, some wires and a small lamp from her brother's bike. Her brother Omar laughed at her. "A lamp? That's not a real invention!" he said. Lina didn't answer and kept working.
On the night before the fair, Lina tested her machine. She pressed the button, but nothing happened. She checked the wires again and again until she was too tired to think.

Jaddi came in with two cups of mint tea. "Let me look," he said. "I was an electrician for forty years, you know." After a minute, he found one loose wire and fixed it, and the little lamp shone bright green. "You did the hard part, my dear," he said. "I only found one small mistake."

At the fair, other students had robots and flying machines, and Lina's lamp looked very small. But when Ms. Noura pressed the button, the green light came on. Then Lina told everyone the story of her grandfather and his friends, and the room became quiet.

Lina didn't win first prize, but she won a special prize for "The Kindest Invention." That evening, the green light flashed in Jaddi's room, and he hurried to open the door. His old friend Abu Fahad was standing there with a big smile. "Finally, Saleh!" he laughed. "I have knocked on this door for a whole year!"

questions.q: Why did Jaddi Saleh's friends often go home sad?
options: He didn't hear them knock on the door.
He was too busy to see them.
He lived far away in another city.

questions.q: What did Ms. Noura ask the students to make?
options: Something that helps a person they love

questions.q: In the story, an "electrician" is a person who…
Why did the lamp not work the night before the fair?
Why do you think the room became quiet when Lina told her story?
options: People were bored with her small lamp.
People were moved by how her invention helped her grandfather.

pages.text: Sara looked out of the plane window. Below, green mountains came up through the white clouds. "We're almost in Abha!" she told her brother, Omar. Their grandmother was waiting for them there.

At the airport, lots of bags moved slowly round and round. Sara saw a blue suitcase with a yellow ribbon on the handle. "That's mine," she said, and she quickly pulled it off. Then the family took a taxi to Grandma's house.

Grandma hugged them and made sweet tea. Sara opened her suitcase to find Grandma's present, but then she stopped. There were no clothes inside, only paints, brushes and a thick notebook. "This isn't my bag!" she cried.

The notebook was full of beautiful drawings of mountains, old stone houses and baboons. On the last page, there was a name and a phone number: "Hassan Al-Qahtani, artist." Mum called the number at once, and a worried voice answered. "Thank goodness! I have your bag, and you have all my work from this week!"

The next morning, they met Mr Hassan at a café high on the mountain. He gave Sara her suitcase, and she gave him his. "I'm sorry," Sara said. "Our bags look exactly the same." Mr Hassan smiled. "Don't worry. Your mistake has given me an idea."

He opened his notebook and started to paint quickly. Soon Sara saw her family on the page: Grandma, Mum, Omar and herself, with the clouds below them like a soft white sea. "This is for your grandmother," he said, and he gave Sara the picture.

Now the painting hangs on Grandma's wall, next to the window. Sara's suitcase is different now too. Its handle has a bright red ribbon and a small card with her own drawing of a mountain. Nobody will take it by mistake again!

questions.q: Which city was Sara's family flying to?
What was on the handle of the suitcase Sara took at the airport?
What does "thick" mean in "a thick notebook"?
Why was Mr Hassan worried on the phone?
options: He lost his phone in the taxi.
He missed his plane to Abha.
Sara had his bag with all his work in it.

questions.q: Why did Sara put a new ribbon and card on her suitcase at the end?
options: So people can find her bag easily and not take it by mistake
Because Mr Hassan asked her to
Because her old ribbon was broken

pages.text: Faisal loved football more than anything. But one week before the big school tournament, he fell off his bike and broke his arm. "No football for six weeks," the doctor said.

On the day of the final, Faisal sat on the bench with his arm in a white cast. He felt sad and useless. Then Coach Hamad sat next to him and gave him a small notebook. "You can't play today, but you can still help," he said. "Watch the other team carefully and write down everything you see."
Faisal watched every move. The other team was fast and strong, and they scored first. Faisal wrote quickly: "Number 9 never shoots. He always passes. Their goalkeeper always jumps to his right."

At half-time, the players looked tired and worried. Faisal opened his notebook and showed them. "Their goalkeeper jumps to his right every time," he said. Omar, the captain, smiled for the first time that day. "Good eyes, Faisal!"

In the second half, Omar scored, and it was 1-1. Then, in the last minute, a player fell in front of the goal, and the referee blew his whistle. Penalty! Omar ran to the bench and asked, "Which side, Faisal?" "His left!" Faisal said. "Shoot to his left!"
Omar ran and kicked the ball hard. The goalkeeper jumped to his right, but the ball flew into the other corner. Goal! The crowd cheered, and the whole team ran to Faisal.

After the game, the players lifted the trophy, and they wrote their names on Faisal's cast. "Next year you'll play again," Coach Hamad said. "But today, you were our secret weapon." Faisal laughed, because he never knew a notebook could win a match.

options: He was late for the game.
The coach was angry with him.

questions.q: What did Coach Hamad give Faisal?

options: He always jumped to his left.
He always jumped to his right.

questions.q: In the story, "cheered" means:
